Subcarrier Shortlist

Which of the 52 subcarriers are worth keeping — measured across walking, mixed activity, standing and sitting, in two different rooms. The short answer is eight, and they are not the ones a per-activity ranking would pick.

Cutting 52 → 8 does not cost accuracy. It buys it. Dropping the band-edge subcarriers removes inputs that carry noise instead of signal, and cross-person accuracy rises +16% — from 42% to 58%. You also cut the feature vector by 85%.
Per activity

Top subcarriers for each activity

This is the ranking you asked for: for each activity, the subcarriers that best separate it from the other three. Scores are one-vs-rest separability (2·|AUC−½| over seven window features), computed per person and then combined.

Each activity really does favour a different part of the band. Walking peaks around SC26–28 and SC36–39; standing sits low (SC4–8, SC18–23); sitting favours the extreme edges (SC2–5, SC40–44).

Do not deploy these per-activity lists. They are honest measurements of the captures you have, but the next column shows they do not survive a change of room — and the reliability test in the next section shows they do not even survive a change of person in the same room. Use them to understand the data, not to configure a receiver.

The same measurement, split by room. If the ranking were a property of the activity, the bright columns would line up vertically between each pair of rows. They do not.

Reliability

What transfers and what doesn't

Before trusting any ranking, it is worth asking whether it is measuring something real or just fitting one recording. Three tiers answer that: split a single capture in half and compare, compare two people in the same room, then compare rooms.

Left: the per-activity separability ranking is highly repeatable inside one capture (ρ = 0.78–0.91) and then collapses — it is negatively correlated between two people in the same room. Right: the motion-SNR profile behaves the opposite way for walking, holding at ρ = +0.81 across people and +0.91 across rooms.

That split is the whole result. A subcarrier's ability to separate this sitting capture from this standing capture is a fact about one afternoon's multipath. How strongly a subcarrier responds to a body moving is a fact about the radio, and it is stable. The recommended set is built only from the second kind.

Mechanism

Why those subcarriers

The amplitude profile is a smooth 15.3 dB arch peaking at band centre, and it is the same arch in both rooms (r ≈ 0.9). Room multipath would be jagged and room-specific; this is the radio's own passband roll-off. Band-edge subcarriers arrive ~15 dB weaker before anyone moves.

Motion response follows that passband almost exactly (ρ = 0.91 against the level profile). For walking the profile is effectively identical in every capture — three people, two rooms, four days apart.

The mechanism, directly. SC29 and SC3 record the same walk with the same energy in the 0.5–25 Hz body-motion band — SC3 is not blind to the motion. SC3 simply carries about 6 dB more noise underneath it, because it sits down in the roll-off. Selecting subcarriers here is selecting SNR, not selecting sensitivity.

Adjacent subcarriers are near-duplicates: correlation falls below 0.5 only after 4 subcarriers, so the 52 carry roughly 13 independent looks at the channel. That is the ceiling on what more subcarriers can buy.

Validation

Does the set actually work

A random forest over the same seven window features, trained on two people and tested on the third — so holding out Gowreesh is simultaneously the cross-room test. Nothing about the test person is seen during training.

The selected set beats a random set of the same size at every size, peaks at 8 subcarriers, and beats all 52. The green line is the same model scored inside the capture it trained on — the gap between green and blue is how much of the usual CSI accuracy is really session memorisation.

Forcing the set to spread across the band makes it worse

The intuitive move is to spread picks across the spectrum for diversity. Tested directly, it loses: requiring 4 subcarriers of spacing drops accuracy to 44% and uniform decimation to 45%, against 58% for the clustered high-SNR set. The SNR you give up at the band edges costs more than the decorrelation buys.

Walking is solid at 87%. Mixed activity mostly collapses into walking, which is reasonable — it contains walking. Sitting and standing are only partly separable from each other. Collapsed to the binary action / no-action question the pilot was built for, this reaches 83% on an unseen person.

Limits

What this data cannot tell you

  • Each activity is one continuous capture per person. Activity is perfectly confounded with recording session, so any slow channel drift is available to the classifier as a shortcut. This is why the same-capture numbers reach 94% while cross-person sits near 55%. Treat the 58% as the honest figure and the 94% as unusable.
  • Environment B is a noisier link. Gowreesh's captures needed 8–11% of samples de-spiked against 0.2–6.5% in env A, and his static sitting capture carries as much 0.5–4 Hz band power as env A's motion captures. Something was moving, or the link was worse. He is also the hardest hold-out (32% at k=8 against 86% for Amrith).
  • Three people, one session each. Enough to show the per-activity ranking does not transfer; not enough to certify the recommended set as final. It is the best-supported choice available, not a proven optimum.
  • Sit and stand rankings are the weakest. Both are near-static, so their profiles are dominated by whatever noise the link had that day (ρ ≤ +0.32 across rooms).
  • Packet arrival is bursty — 65–90 Hz median with gaps. Everything was resampled to a uniform 80 Hz grid, so the 30–38 Hz "noise band" includes some interpolation artefact. It is applied identically to every capture, so comparisons hold.
  • Index-to-frequency mapping is inferred. SC0–51 are assumed to run −26…−1, +1…+26 — supported by the single smooth arch with both ends lowest. On that mapping the core 8 span roughly −1.9 to +1.6 MHz around 2.462 GHz.

If you re-run the capture

Two changes would let this analysis answer much more. Record the activities interleaved within one session rather than as one capture each, which breaks the session confound. And record at least one repeat session per person on a different day — that is the only way to tell a stable subcarrier preference from an afternoon's multipath.

Measured from the 12 pilot captures in data/pilot/. Pipeline: analysis/sc_features.py → sc_select.py → sc_figures.py → sc_report.py; all numbers in analysis/sc_scores.json. Every figure and figure caption is generated from the measured data.
